items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The ability of a material to be drawn out into a wire"?
items.answer: ductility
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of ductility.

items.stem: Priya writes: "A metallic bond is a bond between two metal atoms." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Metallic bonding is non-directional: it is the attraction between all the cations and the sea of delocalised electrons throughout the lattice.
items.markingKey: Metallic bonding is non-directional: it is the attraction between all the cations and the sea of delocalised electrons throughout the lattice. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between ionic bonding and metallic bonding.
items.answer: Metallic bonding is the attraction between cations and delocalised electrons (non-directional, allows malleability); ionic bonding is the attraction between oppositely charged ions in a fixed lattice (brittle).
items.markingKey: Metallic bonding is the attraction between cations and delocalised electrons (non-directional, allows malleability); ionic bonding is the attraction between oppositely charged ions in a fixed lattice (brittle). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: State the oxidation state of iron in FeSO₄. (HL)
items.markingKey: Sum of oxidation states = 0 with K +1, O −2, Cl −1, SO₄ −2: Fe = +2 (1).

items.stem: Which metal has the highest melting point?
items.answer: chromium
items.markingKey: A. Melting points / °C: Cr 1907, Mg 650, Li 181, K 63. Stronger metallic bonding: smaller, more highly charged cations with more delocalised electrons (d electrons in transition metals).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The “sea of electrons” model fully explains the properties of metals."
items.answer: A useful qualitative model with limitations that band theory addresses.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains conductivity, malleability, ductility and lustre qualitatively; explains melting point trends using charge density. Arguments against: cannot explain why some metals are much better conductors than others; does not explain magnetism or the semiconductor behaviour of metalloids; band theory is needed for a quantitative picture. Supported judgement: A useful qualitative model with limitations that band theory addresses.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "transition element"?
options: A polymer formed when monomers with two functional groups join with the loss of a small molecule such as water or HCl at each link
An inorganic, non-metallic solid (often ionic/covalent oxides, carbides or nitrides) that is hard, brittle and heat resistant
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually metals), with metallic bonding, e.g. steel, brass, bronze
An element that has an incomplete d sublevel in its atom or in one of its common ions
items.answer: An element that has an incomplete d sublevel in its atom or in one of its common ions
items.markingKey: D. "transition element" is an element that has an incomplete d sublevel in its atom or in one of its common ions.

items.stem: Define the term "delocalised electrons".
items.answer: Valence electrons that are not associated with a particular atom and can move throughout the metal lattice
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: valence electrons that are not associated with a particular atom and can move throughout the metal lattice. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why metals are malleable.
items.answer: The layers of cations can slide over one another when a force is applied; the delocalised electrons move with them and continue to hold the lattice together, so the metal changes shape without breaking.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The layers of cations can slide over one another when a force is applied; the delocalised electrons move with them and continue to hold the lattice together, so the metal changes shape without breaking. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which metal has the strongest metallic bonding?
items.answer: aluminium
items.markingKey: B. Al³⁺: highest charge density, three electrons delocalised.

items.stem: Strontium melts at 777 °C and aluminium at 660 °C. Explain the difference in terms of metallic bonding.
items.answer: Both form 2+ ions, but Sr has a smaller ionic radius, so its cations are closer to the delocalised electrons, giving stronger metallic bonding.
items.markingKey: both form 2+ ions, but Sr has a smaller ionic radius, so its cations are closer to the delocalised electrons (1); stronger electrostatic attraction between cations and delocalised electrons in Sr (1); more energy needed to break the lattice (1).

items.stem: In the compound CuSO₄, the oxidation state of the transition element is
items.markingKey: B. Oxidation states sum to zero (K +1, O −2, Cl −1, SO₄ −2), so Cu = +2.

items.stem: Which of the metals aluminium, copper, potassium and titanium has the lowest melting point?
items.answer: potassium
items.markingKey: B. Melting points / °C: Al 660, Cu 1085, K 63, Ti 1668. Metallic bonding is stronger for smaller, more highly charged cations with more delocalised electrons.

items.stem: What is the ground-state electron configuration of the iron ion Fe³⁺?
items.answer: [Ar] 3d⁵
items.markingKey: B. Fe: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². The 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons, giving [Ar] 3d⁵.

items.stem: (a) Describe the bonding in aluminium and sodium. (b) Explain, with reference to their melting points (660 °C and 98 °C), which has the stronger metallic bonding. (c) Explain why both metals conduct electricity and heat. (d) Discuss one factor, other than conductivity, that determines whether a metal is suitable for saucepans.
items.answer: (b) aluminium
items.markingKey: (a) lattice of cations in a sea of delocalised electrons (A1). (b) aluminium: higher charge/smaller cation/more delocalised electrons (R1 R1). (c) delocalised electrons move and carry charge/energy (R1). (d) e.g. density, cost, reactivity/corrosion, melting point, strength (R1).

items.stem: Explain the trend in the melting points of sodium (98 °C), magnesium (650 °C) and aluminium (660 °C), and suggest why aluminium is used for overhead power cables while sodium is not.
items.answer: Increasing cation charge (1+, 2+, 3+), decreasing radius and more delocalised electrons per atom across the period → stronger metallic bonding (Al and Mg similar in practice). Aluminium: good conductor, low density, corrosion resistant (oxide layer), strong enough; sodium reacts violently with water and is soft.
items.markingKey: Increasing cation charge (1+, 2+, 3+), decreasing radius and more delocalised electrons per atom across the period → stronger metallic bonding (Al and Mg similar in practice). items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The idea that bonding varies gradually between the ideal ionic, covalent and metallic types rather than falling into distinct categories"?
items.answer: bonding continuum

items.stem: A student claims: "Every compound of a metal with a non-metal is purely ionic." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Bonding is a continuum: e.g. AlCl₃ (ΔX 1.6) has substantial covalent character; pure ionic bonding is an idealisation.
items.markingKey: Bonding is a continuum: e.g. AlCl₃ (ΔX 1.6) has substantial covalent character; pure ionic bonding is an idealisation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between polar covalent bonding and ionic bonding.
items.answer: Ionic bonding involves (near-)complete electron transfer at large ΔX; polar covalent bonding involves unequal sharing at moderate ΔX – they lie at different points on a continuum.
items.markingKey: Ionic bonding involves (near-)complete electron transfer at large ΔX; polar covalent bonding involves unequal sharing at moderate ΔX – they lie at different points on a continuum. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.markingKey: X(Cu) = 1.9, X(Cu) = 1.9 (1); average 1.90 and ΔX 0.0 (1); metallic region (1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The bonding triangle is a better model than classifying substances as simply ionic, covalent or metallic."
items.answer: It is more nuanced and predictive, though still a model with limitations – useful together with structural information.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows bonding as a continuum; predicts intermediate properties (e.g. AlCl₃, SiO₂); quantitative and data based. Arguments against: only applies to binary compounds; electronegativity is itself an approximate scale; does not capture structure (molecular vs network). Supported judgement: It is more nuanced and predictive, though still a model with limitations – useful together with structural information.

items.stem: Explain why properties such as melting point and conductivity change gradually across the bonding triangle.
items.answer: Bonding changes continuously with ΔX and average X, so the degree of electron transfer, sharing or delocalisation, and therefore the properties, vary gradually rather than abruptly.

items.stem: Explain the difference between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.
items.answer: Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers via their C=C bonds with no by-product; condensation polymerisation joins monomers with two functional groups each, eliminating a small molecule (e.g. H₂O) at each link.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Plastics have done more harm than good to the environment."
items.answer: Plastics bring major benefits; the harm stems mainly from single-use design and poor waste management – solutions lie in reduction, recycling and biodegradable alternatives.

items.stem: "The bonding triangle is a better model than classifying substances as simply ionic, covalent or metallic." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: It is more nuanced and predictive, though still a model with limitations – useful together with structural information.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows bonding as a continuum; predicts intermediate properties (e.g. AlCl₃, SiO₂); quantitative and data based. Arguments against: only applies to binary compounds; electronegativity is itself an approximate scale; does not capture structure (molecular vs network). Supported judgement: It is more nuanced and predictive, though still a model with limitations – useful together with structural information. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Compare the formation of poly(1,1-dichloroethene) and PET. (a) Name the type of polymerisation in each and write the repeating unit of poly(1,1-dichloroethene). (b) State the small molecule eliminated, if any, in each. (c) Explain why PET can be hydrolysed (broken down by water/acid) while poly(1,1-dichloroethene) cannot. (d) Evaluate one environmental consequence of the widespread use of poly(1,1-dichloroethene).
items.answer: (a) addition (–CH₂–CCl₂–); condensation; (b) none; water; (c) ester links are polar and can be hydrolysed; C–C backbone cannot
items.markingKey: (a) addition, repeating unit –CH₂–CCl₂–; condensation (A1 A1). (b) none for addition, H₂O for PET (A1). (c) ester linkage contains polar C=O/C–N(O) bonds attacked by water; only strong non-polar C–C/C–H in poly(1,1-dichloroethene) (R1). (d) persistence in landfill/oceans or CO₂/toxic gases on incineration; recycling as mitigation (R1).

items.stem: "The properties of a material can be predicted entirely from its type of bonding." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Bonding is a key starting point, but structure, composition and processing must also be considered.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: bonding explains conductivity, melting point, hardness, brittleness; the bonding triangle links composition to properties. Arguments against: structure (molecular vs network, crystal size, defects) is equally important; composites and nanomaterials have properties not shown by components; processing (heat treatment, alignment of polymer chains) changes properties. Supported judgement: Bonding is a key starting point, but structure, composition and processing must also be considered. Markbands (12 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The ability of a material to be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking"?
items.answer: malleability
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of malleability.

items.stem: Which quantity is plotted on the vertical axis of the bonding triangle in the data booklet?
items.answer: difference in electronegativity, ΔX
items.markingKey: D. x-axis: average X; y-axis: ΔX.

items.stem: Which linkage is present in polyesters such as PET?
items.answer: –COO– (ester)
items.markingKey: C. Formed from diols and dicarboxylic acids.

items.stem: A student claims: "Composites are simply alloys of polymers." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A composite contains distinct phases (matrix + reinforcement) that remain separate; an alloy is a metallic mixture with metallic bonding.
items.markingKey: A composite contains distinct phases (matrix + reinforcement) that remain separate; an alloy is a metallic mixture with metallic bonding. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "A metallic bond is a bond between two metal atoms." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Metallic bonding is non-directional: it is the attraction between all the cations and the sea of delocalised electrons throughout the lattice.
items.markingKey: Metallic bonding is non-directional: it is the attraction between all the cations and the sea of delocalised electrons throughout the lattice. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which compound would show the most covalent character?
items.answer: AlI₃
items.markingKey: A. Smallest ΔX (1.1) and highly polarisable I⁻.

items.stem: Distinguish between condensation polymerisation and addition polymerisation.
items.answer: Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers via their C=C bonds with no by-product; condensation polymerisation joins monomers with two functional groups each, eliminating a small molecule (e.g. H₂O) at each link.
items.markingKey: Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers via their C=C bonds with no by-product; condensation polymerisation joins monomers with two functional groups each, eliminating a small molecule (e.g. H₂O) at each link. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why reinforced concrete is a better structural material than concrete alone.
items.answer: Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension; steel bars have high tensile strength, so the composite resists both compression and tension.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension; steel bars have high tensile strength, so the composite resists both compression and tension. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why metals are good thermal conductors.
items.answer: Delocalised electrons can move freely and transfer kinetic energy rapidly through the lattice, in addition to vibrations of the ions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Delocalised electrons can move freely and transfer kinetic energy rapidly through the lattice, in addition to vibrations of the ions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using electronegativity values from the data booklet, calculate the average electronegativity and the electronegativity difference for NH₃, and deduce its position on the bonding triangle.
items.answer: average X = 2.60, ΔX = 0.8; polar covalent
items.markingKey: X(N) = 3.0, X(H) = 2.2 (1); average 2.60 and ΔX 0.8 (1); polar covalent region (1).

items.stem: 18-carat gold has the mass composition 75 % Au, 12.5 % Ag, 12.5 % Cu. Calculate the number of Cu atoms in 25.0 g of the alloy.
Explain why copper is used for a material for electrical wiring.
items.answer: copper: metallic bonding with delocalised electrons – excellent conductor, ductile.
items.markingKey: copper (1); property needed for the use (1); linked to bonding/structure: metallic bonding with delocalised electrons – excellent conductor, ductile (1).

items.stem: Which of the metals iron, potassium, sodium and strontium has the highest melting point?
items.answer: iron
items.markingKey: B. Melting points / °C: Fe 1538, K 63, Na 98, Sr 777. Metallic bonding is stronger for smaller, more highly charged cations with more delocalised electrons.

items.stem: Sana writes: "Every compound of a metal with a non-metal is purely ionic." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Bonding is a continuum: e.g. AlCl₃ (ΔX 1.6) has substantial covalent character; pure ionic bonding is an idealisation.
items.markingKey: Bonding is a continuum: e.g. AlCl₃ (ΔX 1.6) has substantial covalent character; pure ionic bonding is an idealisation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Duralumin has the mass composition 94 % Al, 4 % Cu, 1 % Mg, 1 % Mn. Calculate the number of Mn atoms in 100 g of the alloy.
A solid material X melts at 3588 °C, is very hard and does not conduct electricity in any state. Which type of bonding and structure is X most likely to have?
items.answer: covalent network
items.markingKey: D. melts at 3588 °C, is very hard, does not conduct electricity in any state → covalent network: giant lattice of strong covalent bonds.

items.stem: (a) Describe the bonding in strontium and potassium. (b) Explain, with reference to their melting points (777 °C and 63 °C), which has the stronger metallic bonding. (c) Explain why both metals conduct electricity and heat. (d) Discuss one factor, other than conductivity, that determines whether a metal is suitable for overhead power cables.
items.answer: (b) strontium
items.markingKey: (a) lattice of cations in a sea of delocalised electrons (A1). (b) strontium: higher charge/smaller cation/more delocalised electrons (R1 R1). (c) delocalised electrons move and carry charge/energy (R1). (d) e.g. density, cost, reactivity/corrosion, melting point, strength (R1).

items.stem: Using the bonding triangle, compare the bonding in CaF₂ and CH₄. (a) Calculate the coordinates of each. (b) Deduce the predominant bonding. (c) Predict one physical property of each that follows from its bonding and explain it.
items.answer: CaF₂: (2.50, 3.0) ionic; CH₄: (2.40, 0.4) covalent
items.markingKey: (a) coordinates (A1 A1). (b) ionic and covalent (A1). (c) one property each linked to bonding, e.g. conductivity, melting point, malleability, solubility (R1 R1).

items.stem: "Bioplastics are the solution to plastic pollution." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: They help in some applications but are not a complete solution; reduction and better recycling remain essential.
